objectives: Hear and identify the initial /y/ sound.
Distinguish /y/ from previously taught initial consonants.
Recognize /y/ at the beginning of simple taught words.
concepts: Initial phonemes occur at the beginning of a word.
The grapheme y can represent /y/ at the beginning of a word.
Careful listening supports accurate sound-to-letter mapping.
Contrasting similar initial sounds improves discrimination.

definitions.definition: The smallest sound unit that can distinguish words.
A letter or group of letters representing a sound.
The first phoneme heard in a word.

workedExamples: yam begins /y/ and is written with initial y.
yet begins /y/; listen before selecting the first letter.
yes begins /y/, so the initial grapheme is y.
commonMistakes: Choosing w because it is a familiar consonant.
Listening to the vowel instead of the initial sound.
Naming the letter without producing its sound.

conceptual: Contrast /y/ with /w/, /j/ and other taught initial sounds.
application: Map initial /y/ to grapheme y in new words.
higherOrderThinking: Explain why the first sound determines the initial grapheme.
mixedReview: Mix /y/ recognition with previously taught consonants.

quickRevision: hear → identify /y/ → say /y/ → map to y
mistakeBasedRevision: If /y/ is confused with another sound, repeat the contrast pair slowly and attend to the first phoneme.
weakTopicRevision: Practise /y/ versus the specific consonant causing confusion.

outcomes: Learner distinguishes /y/ from previously taught consonants.
Learner maps initial /y/ to grapheme y.

questions.question: Which letter represents the /y/ sound at the beginning of 'yes'?
Which word does NOT begin with /y/?
Which pair begins with the same sound?
What sound do you hear first in 'yak'?
What sound do you hear first in 'yet'?
Which grapheme should you write for the initial sound in 'yam'?
Why do we listen for the first sound before choosing a letter?
options: to map the phoneme to the correct grapheme

questions.question: A learner hears /y/ in 'yes' but writes w. What needs practice?
Which word provides a clear initial /y/ contrast with 'wet'?
After identifying /y/, what should the learner do?
options: connect the sound to grapheme y and say it again
